title: Unreliable Narrator
definition: A storyteller whose account cannot be fully trusted.
explanation: The narrator may distort events because of bias, limited knowledge, memory gaps, self-deception, emotional instability, or deliberate dishonesty. Readers must compare what the narrator says with clues in the story to understand what may actually be happening.
example: Stevens in The Remains of the Day minimizes his regrets, while the reader gradually recognizes the emotions and choices he refuses to confront.

title: Foreshadowing
definition: An early hint that suggests something important will happen later.
explanation: Foreshadowing can appear through dialogue, objects, weather, recurring imagery, unusual details, or seemingly casual comments. It prepares the reader for later events without revealing them directly.
example: A character repeatedly noticing a damaged bridge may signal that the bridge will become important later in the story.

title: Flashback
definition: A scene that moves the story back to an earlier event.
explanation: Flashbacks reveal information about a character’s past, explain motivations, deepen relationships, or provide context that changes how the present storyline is understood.
example: A detective remembers a childhood incident that explains why a current case feels personally important.

title: Flashforward
definition: A scene that temporarily shows events from the future.
explanation: Flashforwards can create anticipation, mystery, or dramatic tension by giving the reader a glimpse of what may happen before returning to the present timeline.
example: A novel opens with the protagonist standing alone at a train station ten years later, then returns to the beginning of the story.

title: Epistolary Novel
definition: A story told through letters, messages, journals, or documents.
explanation: Epistolary fiction presents events through written records created by characters. This format often creates intimacy while also limiting the reader to incomplete or subjective information.
example: A novel may tell its entire story through emails exchanged between two characters who never meet in person.

title: Stream of Consciousness
definition: Writing that follows a character’s continuous flow of thoughts.
explanation: This technique imitates the way thoughts move naturally between memories, sensations, emotions, observations, and associations. Grammar and chronology may become less structured as the reader experiences the character’s mind directly.
example: A character walking home may move rapidly from noticing traffic to remembering childhood, worrying about tomorrow, and recalling a song.

title: Magical Realism
definition: Realistic fiction where magical events are treated as ordinary.
explanation: Magical realism places supernatural or impossible elements inside an otherwise recognizable world. Characters usually accept these events without the surprise expected in traditional fantasy.
example: A family may calmly accept that one relative has lived for two hundred years as if it were simply part of everyday life.

title: Metafiction
definition: Fiction that draws attention to the fact that it is a constructed story.
explanation: Metafiction may include characters who know they are fictional, narrators who discuss storytelling, or plots that directly question how stories are created and interpreted.
example: A narrator interrupts the story to argue with the reader about whether the ending should be changed.

title: Bildungsroman
definition: A novel focused on a character’s growth from youth toward maturity.
explanation: A Bildungsroman follows emotional, intellectual, social, or moral development. The protagonist usually faces experiences that challenge their beliefs and gradually shape their identity.
example: A young character leaves home, experiences independence and failure, and returns with a more mature understanding of themselves.

title: Dramatic Irony
definition: The reader knows something important that a character does not.
explanation: Dramatic irony creates tension, humor, or tragedy because readers understand the true situation while characters act on incomplete or incorrect information.
example: The reader knows that a visitor is secretly the villain, while the protagonist welcomes them as a trusted friend.

title: Verbal Irony
definition: A speaker says one thing while meaning something different.
explanation: Verbal irony depends on contrast between literal words and intended meaning. Tone, context, and situation help the reader recognize the difference.
example: After being caught in a sudden storm without an umbrella, a character says, “Perfect weather.”

title: Situational Irony
definition: The outcome of a situation is very different from what is expected.
explanation: Situational irony occurs when events produce an unexpected result that contradicts normal assumptions or the expectations established by the story.
example: A professional security expert accidentally locks themselves out of their own house.

title: Motif
definition: A recurring element that supports a larger theme.
explanation: A motif may be an image, object, phrase, color, sound, place, or situation that appears repeatedly and gains meaning through repetition.
example: Repeated references to locked doors may reinforce a story’s theme of isolation and emotional distance.

title: Symbolism
definition: The use of an object, image, or action to represent a deeper idea.
explanation: Symbols add additional layers of meaning beyond their literal role in the story. Their significance often develops through context and repetition.
example: A dying garden may symbolize the deterioration of a family relationship.

title: Allegory
definition: A story in which characters and events represent broader ideas.
explanation: Allegories operate on two levels: the literal story and a symbolic meaning connected to politics, morality, philosophy, religion, or society.
example: A fictional society of animals may represent different social classes or political groups.

title: Archetype
definition: A recurring character type, symbol, or pattern found across many stories.
explanation: Archetypes are recognizable narrative models such as the mentor, rebel, hero, trickster, or journey into the unknown. Writers can follow, modify, or deliberately subvert them.
example: An experienced guide who prepares the protagonist for a dangerous journey represents the mentor archetype.

title: Antihero
definition: A central character who lacks traditional heroic qualities.
explanation: Antiheroes may be selfish, dishonest, fearful, cynical, or morally complicated while still remaining the main character whose journey drives the story.
example: A thief who helps others only when it benefits them may still become the protagonist readers follow.

title: Foil Character
definition: A character whose qualities contrast with another character.
explanation: A foil makes another character’s personality, values, strengths, or weaknesses easier to recognize by presenting an opposing set of traits.
example: A highly cautious friend may highlight the protagonist’s impulsive personality.

title: Character Arc
definition: The internal development a character experiences across a story.
explanation: A character arc tracks how beliefs, behavior, relationships, or identity change because of events in the narrative. Some characters grow positively, while others decline or remain deliberately unchanged.
example: A character who begins afraid of responsibility may gradually learn to lead others confidently.

title: Point of View
definition: The perspective from which a story is told.
explanation: Point of view determines what information the reader receives and how closely they experience a character’s thoughts. Common forms include first person, second person, third-person limited, and third-person omniscient.
example: A first-person narrator can describe only what they personally know, remember, or believe.

title: Third-Person Limited
definition: A narrator follows one character’s perspective at a time.
explanation: The story uses third-person pronouns while giving readers access primarily to one character’s thoughts, emotions, and observations. Other characters remain partly mysterious.
example: The narrator can describe what Maya thinks about the argument but cannot directly reveal what her brother is thinking.

title: Third-Person Omniscient
definition: A narrator can access multiple characters’ thoughts and information.
explanation: An omniscient narrator may move between characters, reveal events happening elsewhere, provide historical context, or explain information that no single character knows.
example: One chapter may reveal both sides of an argument by showing what each character privately believes.

title: In Medias Res
definition: A story that begins in the middle of ongoing action.
explanation: Instead of starting with background information, the narrative places the reader directly inside an important event and explains earlier circumstances later.
example: A novel begins with the protagonist escaping from a burning building before explaining how the fire started.

title: Frame Narrative
definition: A story that contains another story within it.
explanation: A frame narrative uses an outer storyline to introduce or surround one or more inner stories. The relationship between these layers can influence how readers interpret the events.
example: Travelers gather during a journey and each tells a different story.

title: Circular Narrative
definition: A story that ends in a place or situation similar to where it began.
explanation: Circular narratives create a sense of completion, repetition, inevitability, or transformation by returning to an earlier image, setting, phrase, or event.
example: A novel begins and ends at the same train station, but the protagonist understands the place completely differently at the end.

title: Cliffhanger
definition: An unresolved moment designed to create strong anticipation.
explanation: Cliffhangers often end chapters, episodes, or sections at a moment of danger, discovery, or uncertainty, encouraging the reader to continue immediately.
example: A chapter ends just as the protagonist opens a letter that could reveal who betrayed them.

title: Red Herring
definition: A misleading clue intended to distract from the truth.
explanation: Red herrings direct attention toward an incorrect suspect, explanation, or solution while preserving the real answer for later.
example: Suspicious fingerprints appear to identify one suspect, but they later prove unrelated to the crime.

title: MacGuffin
definition: An object or goal that motivates the plot more than it matters itself.
explanation: A MacGuffin gives characters something to pursue, protect, recover, or discover. Its exact nature may be less important than the conflict it creates.
example: Several characters compete to find a mysterious briefcase, although the story never reveals what is inside.

title: Chekhov’s Gun
definition: An important detail introduced early should later have a purpose.
explanation: The principle suggests that prominent narrative elements should contribute meaningfully to the story rather than existing without consequence.
example: If a broken key is carefully mentioned in the first chapter, it may later become essential to solving the central mystery.

title: Deus Ex Machina
definition: A sudden unexpected solution that resolves a difficult conflict.
explanation: This device occurs when a problem is solved by an unlikely event, new character, ability, or piece of information that was not adequately prepared earlier in the story.
example: Just before the heroes lose, an unknown relative suddenly arrives with exactly the evidence needed to solve everything.

title: Prologue
definition: An opening section that appears before the main story begins.
explanation: A prologue provides information the reader may need before entering the central narrative. It can introduce an earlier event, establish the world, present a mystery, or show a scene from a different perspective.
example: A fantasy novel opens with an ancient battle that took place centuries before the protagonist was born.

title: Epilogue
definition: A closing section that shows what happens after the main story ends.
explanation: An epilogue gives readers additional resolution by revealing the later lives of characters, the long-term consequences of events, or the state of the world after the central conflict is over.
example: The final chapter jumps forward ten years to show where the main characters eventually settled.

title: Exposition
definition: The information that introduces the story’s setting, characters, and situation.
explanation: Exposition gives readers the context needed to understand the narrative. It may explain relationships, past events, social rules, or important features of the fictional world.
example: The opening pages establish that the protagonist has recently moved to a remote coastal town after losing their job.

title: Inciting Incident
definition: The event that disrupts normal life and starts the main conflict.
explanation: The inciting incident pushes the protagonist into the central story. It creates a problem, opportunity, discovery, or decision that makes returning to the previous status quo difficult.
example: A character receives a letter revealing that a family member they believed was dead may still be alive.

title: Rising Action
definition: A sequence of events that increases conflict and tension.
explanation: Rising action develops after the story’s central problem has been introduced. Obstacles grow more difficult, relationships become complicated, and the consequences of failure become more serious.
example: Each attempt to solve a mystery creates new suspects and exposes increasingly dangerous secrets.

title: Climax
definition: The most intense turning point of the story.
explanation: The climax usually brings the central conflict to its highest level of tension. The protagonist must often make an important decision, confront a major opponent, or face the consequences of earlier choices.
example: The protagonist finally confronts the person responsible for the central conspiracy.

title: Falling Action
definition: Events that occur after the climax as the conflict begins to settle.
explanation: Falling action shows the immediate consequences of the story’s major turning point and starts resolving remaining questions or secondary conflicts.
example: After the final confrontation, the characters return home and begin repairing the relationships damaged during the conflict.

title: Resolution
definition: The part of the story where the main conflicts reach an ending.
explanation: Resolution explains what remains after the climax and shows how the events have changed the characters or their circumstances. It can be complete, ambiguous, or intentionally open.
example: The protagonist accepts a new life after finally resolving the family conflict that drove the story.

title: Open Ending
definition: An ending that leaves important questions unresolved.
explanation: Open endings deliberately avoid providing a definitive answer about what happens next. They encourage the reader to interpret the final events and imagine possible outcomes.
example: The novel ends as the character approaches an unknown destination without revealing whether they will stay or leave.

title: Twist Ending
definition: A final revelation that significantly changes the meaning of earlier events.
explanation: A strong twist ending surprises the reader while still being supported by clues that become understandable in retrospect.
example: The final scene reveals that the person investigating the disappearance unknowingly caused it.

title: Ambiguous Ending
definition: An ending that supports more than one reasonable interpretation.
explanation: Ambiguous endings provide enough information for readers to form theories but deliberately avoid confirming a single explanation.
example: The final image can be read either as proof that the supernatural event was real or as evidence of the protagonist’s imagination.

title: Plot Twist
definition: An unexpected development that changes the direction or interpretation of the story.
explanation: Plot twists overturn assumptions about characters, motives, events, or the central conflict. Effective twists usually have earlier clues that become meaningful afterward.
example: A trusted ally is revealed to have been secretly working for the antagonist.

title: Subplot
definition: A secondary storyline that develops alongside the main plot.
explanation: Subplots can deepen characters, explore additional themes, introduce contrast, or eventually connect with the central conflict.
example: While solving the main mystery, the protagonist also struggles to repair a damaged relationship with a sibling.

title: Parallel Plot
definition: Two or more storylines that develop alongside each other.
explanation: Parallel plots may follow different characters, locations, or time periods. Their similarities and differences often create additional meaning before the storylines eventually intersect.
example: One storyline follows a scientist in the present while another follows the scientist’s ancestor a century earlier.

title: Nonlinear Narrative
definition: A story told in an order that does not follow straightforward chronology.
explanation: Nonlinear narratives may jump between time periods, repeat events from different viewpoints, or reveal consequences before causes.
example: The reader sees the aftermath of a disappearance before learning what happened during the previous week.

title: Multiple Perspectives
definition: A story told through the viewpoints of several characters.
explanation: Multiple perspectives allow readers to experience the same events through different beliefs, motivations, and levels of knowledge. Contradictions between narrators can become important to the plot.
example: Alternating chapters show how two siblings remember the same childhood event very differently.

title: Second-Person Narration
definition: A narrative that addresses the protagonist as “you.”
explanation: Second-person narration places the reader in an unusual relationship with the character by describing actions and experiences as if they belong directly to “you.”
example: “You open the door even though you already know who is waiting on the other side.”

title: Free Indirect Discourse
definition: Third-person narration that blends closely with a character’s own thoughts and voice.
explanation: Free indirect discourse allows narration to adopt a character’s vocabulary, opinions, and emotional perspective without using quotation marks or phrases such as “she thought.”
example: He looked at the empty chair. Of course she had left. Why would anyone stay?

title: Interior Monologue
definition: Direct presentation of a character’s private thoughts.
explanation: Interior monologue gives readers access to the internal reasoning, memories, fears, or reactions of a character, often in a more structured form than stream of consciousness.
example: A character silently rehearses every possible response before entering an important meeting.

title: Narrative Voice
definition: The distinctive personality and style through which a story is told.
explanation: Narrative voice is shaped by vocabulary, rhythm, attitude, humor, formality, and perspective. Two narrators can describe the same event in completely different ways.
example: One narrator describes a city with cynical humor, while another presents the same streets with nostalgic affection.

title: Tone
definition: The attitude expressed by the narrator or author toward the subject.
explanation: Tone can feel playful, bitter, formal, intimate, sarcastic, melancholic, hopeful, or threatening. It is created through word choice, sentence structure, imagery, and context.
example: A description of an empty house can feel peaceful or disturbing depending on the language used.

title: Mood
definition: The emotional atmosphere a text creates for the reader.
explanation: Mood develops through setting, imagery, pacing, sound, descriptions, and tone. Unlike tone, which reflects an attitude, mood refers primarily to the feeling experienced by the reader.
example: Heavy rain, empty streets, and distant footsteps may create an uneasy mood.

title: Diction
definition: An author’s or character’s choice of words.
explanation: Diction can be formal, conversational, poetic, technical, regional, simple, or highly elaborate. Word choice strongly influences voice, tone, and characterization.
example: A scientist may describe rain as “precipitation,” while a poet describes it as “silver threads.”

title: Syntax
definition: The arrangement and structure of words within sentences.
explanation: Writers use syntax to control rhythm, emphasis, clarity, tension, and pace. Short sentences can create urgency, while long complex sentences can slow the reader down.
example: “Run. Now.” creates a different effect from a long sentence explaining why escape is necessary.

title: Imagery
definition: Language that creates vivid sensory impressions.
explanation: Imagery appeals to sight, sound, touch, smell, taste, or physical sensation, helping readers experience a scene more directly.
example: “The sharp smell of pine mixed with cold smoke from the dying fire.”

title: Metaphor
definition: A comparison that describes one thing as another.
explanation: Metaphor connects two different ideas without using “like” or “as,” allowing one concept to illuminate another.
example: “Her memory was a locked room.”

title: Simile
definition: A comparison using words such as “like” or “as.”
explanation: Similes make descriptions clearer or more vivid by directly comparing one thing with another recognizable image or quality.
example: “The lake was smooth like polished glass.”

title: Personification
definition: Giving human characteristics to nonhuman things.
explanation: Personification allows objects, animals, weather, or abstract ideas to behave as if they possess human emotions or intentions.
example: “The old house watched them from the hill.”

title: Hyperbole
definition: Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or effect.
explanation: Hyperbole is not intended to be interpreted literally. It can intensify emotion, create humor, or emphasize a character’s perspective.
example: “I waited a thousand years for the bus.”

title: Understatement
definition: Deliberately describing something as less important or intense than it really is.
explanation: Understatement can produce humor, irony, emotional restraint, or contrast by minimizing an obviously significant event.
example: After surviving a dangerous storm, a character says, “That was slightly unpleasant.”

title: Oxymoron
definition: A phrase that combines apparently contradictory words.
explanation: Oxymorons bring opposing ideas together to express a complex feeling or unusual concept.
example: “Deafening silence.”

title: Paradox
definition: A statement that seems contradictory but may contain a deeper truth.
explanation: Paradoxes challenge straightforward logic and encourage readers to reconsider assumptions.
example: “The more he learned, the less certain he became.”

title: Allusion
definition: An indirect reference to another work, person, myth, event, or cultural idea.
explanation: Allusions rely on the reader recognizing the reference and connecting its associations to the current text.
example: Calling a difficult journey “an odyssey” alludes to Homer’s Odyssey.

title: Intertextuality
definition: The way one text connects with, responds to, or transforms other texts.
explanation: Intertextuality includes references, adaptations, quotations, structural parallels, retellings, and deliberate conversations between different works.
example: A modern novel retells an ancient myth from the perspective of a previously minor character.

title: Satire
definition: The use of humor or exaggeration to criticize people, institutions, or society.
explanation: Satire exposes flaws by making them appear absurd, contradictory, or ridiculous. It may be playful or sharply political.
example: A fictional bureaucracy requires citizens to complete twenty forms just to request permission to fill out another form.

title: Parody
definition: An imitation that exaggerates recognizable features for comic or critical effect.
explanation: Parody depends on readers recognizing the style, genre, or work being imitated. It often exaggerates familiar conventions.
example: A story imitates detective fiction but gives the investigator increasingly ridiculous clues.

title: Pastiche
definition: A work that intentionally imitates or combines the styles of other works.
explanation: Unlike parody, pastiche is often affectionate rather than mocking. It may celebrate a literary style, genre, or period.
example: A modern mystery is written in the style of nineteenth-century detective fiction.

title: Genre Convention
definition: A familiar feature commonly associated with a particular genre.
explanation: Genre conventions help readers understand what kind of story they are entering. Writers may follow these expectations or deliberately break them.
example: A locked-room mystery typically includes a seemingly impossible crime and a limited group of suspects.

title: Trope
definition: A recognizable storytelling pattern, idea, or recurring convention.
explanation: Tropes are not automatically clichés. They are familiar building blocks that can be used traditionally, combined creatively, or subverted.
example: “Enemies to lovers” is a common relationship trope.

title: Cliché
definition: An expression or idea that has become overly familiar through repeated use.
explanation: Clichés can feel predictable because readers have encountered them many times. Writers sometimes avoid them or deliberately use them for humor or characterization.
example: “It was a dark and stormy night.”

title: Genre Subversion
definition: Deliberately challenging or reversing familiar genre expectations.
explanation: Genre subversion begins with conventions readers recognize and then changes them in an unexpected way.
example: A fantasy story introduces a chosen hero who immediately refuses the quest and never becomes the central savior.

title: Worldbuilding
definition: The creation of the social, physical, cultural, and historical details of a fictional world.
explanation: Worldbuilding can include geography, politics, technology, religion, economics, language, customs, and everyday life. Strong worldbuilding helps fictional settings feel internally consistent.
example: A science-fiction novel establishes how people travel, communicate, work, and govern colonies across several planets.

title: Setting
definition: The time, place, and environment in which a story occurs.
explanation: Setting can influence character behavior, atmosphere, conflict, and theme. It includes both physical location and broader historical or social context.
example: A mystery set in an isolated hotel during a snowstorm creates different possibilities from one set in a crowded city.

title: Atmosphere
definition: The overall feeling created by a story’s environment and presentation.
explanation: Atmosphere combines setting, description, tone, sensory details, and pacing to create a distinctive emotional experience.
example: Flickering lights, empty corridors, and distant sounds create a tense atmosphere.

title: Theme
definition: A central idea or question explored throughout a work.
explanation: Themes are broader than plot. They may concern identity, power, memory, grief, freedom, family, morality, or other recurring human experiences.
example: A novel about several generations may explore how memory shapes family identity.

title: Central Conflict
definition: The main struggle that drives the story forward.
explanation: Conflict can occur between characters, within a character, against society, nature, technology, fate, or another force.
example: A protagonist must decide whether loyalty to their family is more important than revealing a dangerous truth.

title: Internal Conflict
definition: A struggle happening within a character’s thoughts or emotions.
explanation: Internal conflict often involves competing desires, beliefs, fears, responsibilities, or values.
example: A character wants to leave their hometown but feels responsible for caring for a parent.

title: External Conflict
definition: A struggle between a character and an outside force.
explanation: External conflict may involve another person, society, nature, institutions, technology, or physical circumstances.
example: A group of climbers must survive a sudden storm while trying to descend a mountain.

title: Characterization
definition: The methods used to reveal a character’s personality and qualities.
explanation: Characterization may be direct, through explicit description, or indirect, through actions, dialogue, habits, thoughts, and reactions.
example: A character repeatedly giving away their own food reveals generosity without the narrator directly describing them as generous.

title: Indirect Characterization
definition: Revealing a character through behavior rather than direct description.
explanation: Readers infer personality from what a character says, does, thinks, wears, notices, or how others respond to them.
example: A character quietly repairs a stranger’s bicycle without mentioning it afterward, suggesting kindness through action.

title: Direct Characterization
definition: Explicitly telling the reader what a character is like.
explanation: Direct characterization states a character’s personality, appearance, background, or qualities clearly instead of requiring the reader to infer them.
example: “Elena was impatient, ambitious, and deeply afraid of failure.”

title: Flat Character
definition: A character built around a small number of recognizable traits.
explanation: Flat characters usually do not develop significantly during the story. They often support the plot or highlight qualities in more complex characters.
example: A consistently cheerful neighbor appears several times but never changes or reveals deeper motivations.

title: Round Character
definition: A complex character with multiple traits, motives, and contradictions.
explanation: Round characters feel psychologically developed because they possess strengths, weaknesses, changing emotions, and conflicting desires.
example: A generous leader may also be deeply controlling and afraid of losing authority.

title: Dynamic Character
definition: A character who changes significantly during the story.
explanation: The change may involve beliefs, behavior, priorities, relationships, or self-understanding.
example: A cynical character gradually learns to trust other people after being forced to depend on them.

title: Static Character
definition: A character who remains fundamentally unchanged.
explanation: Static characters may experience major events without altering their central beliefs or personality.
example: A stubborn ruler remains convinced of their own judgment despite repeated failures.

title: Protagonist
definition: The central character whose goals drive the main story.
explanation: The protagonist is not necessarily heroic or morally good. They are simply the character around whom the primary conflict is organized.
example: A morally questionable detective can still be the protagonist if the story follows their investigation.

title: Antagonist
definition: A character or force that opposes the protagonist.
explanation: An antagonist may be a villain, rival, institution, social system, natural force, or even the protagonist’s own fear.
example: A corrupt company prevents the protagonist from exposing dangerous information.

title: Deuteragonist
definition: The second most important character in a narrative.
explanation: The deuteragonist often supports, contrasts with, or complicates the protagonist’s journey.
example: A protagonist’s closest friend may have an important parallel storyline and influence major decisions.

title: Confidant
definition: A character trusted with another character’s private thoughts.
explanation: Confidants allow protagonists to express feelings, fears, and plans that might otherwise remain internal.
example: A princess shares her doubts with a childhood friend she trusts completely.

title: Mentor
definition: A figure who guides or teaches another character.
explanation: Mentors may provide knowledge, skills, emotional support, warnings, or tools needed for a difficult journey.
example: An experienced musician helps a younger performer understand both technique and confidence.

title: Tragic Hero
definition: A central character whose downfall is connected to a serious flaw or error.
explanation: Tragic heroes often possess admirable qualities but make choices that contribute to their own destruction.
example: A respected leader’s pride prevents them from admitting a mistake until the consequences become irreversible.

title: Fatal Flaw
definition: A weakness that contributes to a character’s downfall.
explanation: The flaw may be pride, jealousy, ambition, fear, indecision, or another trait that becomes destructive under pressure.
example: A commander’s inability to trust others causes them to reject advice that could save their army.

title: Hubris
definition: Excessive pride or confidence that leads to serious consequences.
explanation: Hubris often causes characters to underestimate danger, ignore warnings, or believe they are beyond ordinary limits.
example: A scientist assumes every risk can be controlled and refuses to stop a dangerous experiment.

title: Catharsis
definition: An emotional release experienced through a powerful story.
explanation: Catharsis is especially associated with tragedy, where intense fear, sorrow, or tension is resolved through the narrative experience.
example: A devastating ending may leave the reader emotionally exhausted but also relieved.

title: Pathos
definition: An appeal designed to evoke strong emotion.
explanation: Pathos may create sympathy, sadness, fear, hope, anger, or compassion through situations, imagery, and character experiences.
example: A child waiting every evening for a parent who will never return creates strong emotional appeal.

title: Ethos
definition: An appeal based on credibility or authority.
explanation: Ethos persuades the audience by presenting the speaker as trustworthy, knowledgeable, experienced, or morally credible.
example: A doctor discussing public health may establish credibility through professional experience.

title: Logos
definition: An appeal based on logic and evidence.
explanation: Logos relies on reasoning, facts, examples, statistics, or cause-and-effect relationships to support an argument.
example: An essay compares data from several studies before reaching a conclusion.

title: Rhetorical Question
definition: A question asked for effect rather than to receive an answer.
explanation: Rhetorical questions can emphasize an argument, provoke reflection, or create emotional impact.
example: “How much longer can we ignore the problem?”

title: Repetition
definition: Deliberate reuse of words, phrases, sounds, or ideas.
explanation: Repetition can create rhythm, reinforce a theme, emphasize emotion, or make an idea memorable.
example: A poem repeatedly begins lines with “I remember” to emphasize memory.

title: Anaphora
definition: Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses.
explanation: Anaphora creates rhythm and emphasis by repeatedly returning to the same opening language.
example: “We waited in silence. We waited in fear. We waited for morning.”

title: Epiphora
definition: Repetition at the end of successive phrases or sentences.
explanation: Epiphora reinforces an idea through repeated endings and can create a strong rhythmic effect.
example: “They wanted justice, demanded justice, and would not leave without justice.”

title: Juxtaposition
definition: Placing contrasting elements close together.
explanation: Juxtaposition highlights differences or unexpected similarities between characters, settings, images, or ideas.
example: A lavish celebration is described immediately beside scenes of poverty outside the palace.

title: Contrast
definition: Emphasizing differences between two elements.
explanation: Contrast can reveal character traits, strengthen themes, or create visual and emotional tension.
example: One sibling values tradition while the other constantly seeks change.

title: Antithesis
definition: Contrasting ideas expressed in a balanced structure.
explanation: Antithesis places opposing concepts side by side to sharpen the difference between them.
example: “She wanted freedom; he wanted control.”

title: Pun
definition: A joke based on multiple meanings or similar-sounding words.
explanation: Puns create humor or clever ambiguity by exploiting the flexibility of language.
example: A baker says business is “on the rise.”

title: Double Entendre
definition: A phrase that can be understood in two different ways.
explanation: One meaning is usually obvious while another may be humorous, ironic, or suggestive.
example: A character says, “That was quite a performance,” referring both to a speech and someone’s dramatic behavior.

title: Ambiguity
definition: Language or events that allow more than one interpretation.
explanation: Writers may use ambiguity deliberately to create uncertainty, complexity, or multiple layers of meaning.
example: A character’s final smile could indicate forgiveness or hidden revenge.

title: Connotation
definition: The emotional or cultural associations connected to a word.
explanation: Connotation goes beyond dictionary meaning and influences how language feels to the reader.
example: “Home” may suggest comfort and belonging beyond simply meaning a place of residence.

title: Denotation
definition: The literal dictionary meaning of a word.
explanation: Denotation refers to the direct meaning without emotional or symbolic associations.
example: The denotation of “snake” is a legless reptile.

title: Euphemism
definition: A softer expression used instead of a harsher one.
explanation: Euphemisms can make difficult, uncomfortable, or sensitive subjects sound less direct.
example: Saying someone “passed away” instead of “died.”

title: Dysphemism
definition: A deliberately harsh or negative expression.
explanation: Dysphemism makes a subject sound more unpleasant, insulting, or emotionally charged.
example: Calling an old building a “wreck” rather than simply “run-down.”

title: Colloquialism
definition: Informal language associated with everyday conversation.
explanation: Colloquialisms can make dialogue sound natural and reveal social, regional, or generational identity.
example: A character says “gonna” or “no big deal” in casual speech.

title: Dialect
definition: A form of language associated with a particular region or social group.
explanation: Dialect can include distinctive pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, and expressions.
example: Characters from different regions may use different words for the same everyday object.

title: Idiolect
definition: The unique way an individual person uses language.
explanation: An idiolect includes characteristic vocabulary, rhythm, grammar, repeated phrases, and speaking habits.
example: One character constantly uses precise technical vocabulary even in casual conversation.

title: Register
definition: The level of formality used in a particular situation.
explanation: Register changes depending on audience, context, profession, and social relationship.
example: A character speaks formally during a job interview but casually with close friends.

title: Alliteration
definition: Repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words.
explanation: Alliteration adds rhythm, emphasis, or musicality to prose and poetry.
example: “Silver streets shimmered silently.”

title: Assonance
definition: Repetition of similar vowel sounds in nearby words.
explanation: Assonance creates subtle musical patterns and can connect words through sound.
example: “The low road rolled home.”

title: Consonance
definition: Repetition of consonant sounds within or at the ends of words.
explanation: Consonance creates rhythm and sonic texture without requiring full rhyme.
example: “Blank and think” repeat the “nk” sound.

title: Onomatopoeia
definition: A word that imitates the sound it describes.
explanation: Onomatopoeia makes writing more sensory by connecting language directly with sound.
example: “Buzz,” “crash,” “whisper,” and “clang.”

title: Rhythm
definition: The pattern and flow created by sounds, stresses, and sentence structure.
explanation: Rhythm influences the speed and emotional effect of prose or poetry. Writers can create smooth, abrupt, repetitive, or highly musical movement through sentence length and sound.
example: Short repeated sentences can create urgency during an action scene.
